AbstractText.Label: AIM
AbstractText.content: Sacral neuromodulation (SNM) is a minimal invasive therapy for functional-constipation (FC) and is most often used to treat adults. Recent studies suggest that SNM may also beneficial in children. However, comparative data regarding preferred age of SNM for FC are lacking. Therefore, long-term results of SNM for FC were compared between children and adults.

AbstractText.Label: METHOD
AbstractText.content: All patients treated with SNM for FC between 2004 and 2015 were evaluated. Outcomes of children (age 10-18 years) were compared with adults (≥18 years). Primary endpoint was a defaecation frequency ≥ 3 times per week which is consistent with the ROME-III criteria. Secondary outcomes were Quality of life (SF-36) and the Cleveland-Clinic-Constipation-Score.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: 180 patients (45 children, 135 adults) were eligible for SNM. Mean age was 15.8 (children) and 41.4 years (adults) respectively. 126 patients received permanent SNM (38 children, 88 adults). Mean follow-up was 47 months in both groups. Defaecation frequency increased in both groups after SNM compared with baseline. Defaecation frequency in adults was higher compared with children. The increased defaecation frequency was maintained during entire follow-up in both groups. QoL of children was impaired compared to the Dutch population regarding bodily pain, general health and vitality. Adults had worse QoL regarding physical functioning, bodily pain, general health, vitality and social functioning compared with the Dutch population. QoL of children did not differ from adults.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: SNM should be considered in children (<18 years) with FC. However, the indication of SNM for FC remains debatable considering the limited improvements and high costs. This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
